passage: Lights-out had already gone in the boys' hostel, but Ojas was still sitting on his bed, turning his torch on and off. Kiran looked up from his bunk. "What's with you?" For a long moment Ojas said nothing. Then, very fast: "My parents are separating. Papa moved out last month. I haven't told anyone." His ears went hot. He waited for a joke. Kiran sat up and swung his legs down. "That's heavy, yaar. You've been carrying that alone?" Ojas nodded, eyes on the floor. "I thought you'd think I was weird." "Why would I?" Kiran said. "My uncle and aunty split. It was rough on my cousin." They talked in whispers until the warden's footsteps passed. Ojas slept better that night than he had in weeks.

qa.q: Who moved out last month, according to Ojas?
qa.a: His Papa moved out.

qa.q: What was Ojas afraid of before he spoke?
qa.a: He feared Kiran would mock him or think he was weird, which is why his ears went hot and he waited for a joke.

qa.q: Which reply from Kiran made opening up feel safe, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether Ojas had carried it alone showed he took it seriously, and sharing his cousin's story made Ojas feel less strange.

qa.q: What would change if Kiran had laughed?
qa.a: Ojas would likely have shut down and kept the secret even longer, feeling more alone and less willing to trust anyone.

grounding: Shows a teen taking the risky step of opening up to a peer about something painful, and the relief when it is received well.

passage:
Hi Yash,

Okay, this is weird to write, so I'm just going to type it before I chicken out.

When you asked on the phone last week how the new school was, I said "amazing, everyone's great." That wasn't true. I eat lunch in the library most days. Nobody's mean, I just haven't found my people, and I miss our gang so much it's embarrassing.

I didn't tell you because I thought you'd feel sorry for me, or think I'd become a loser here. But you're my oldest friend, and pretending with you felt worse than being lonely.

So, yeah. That's the truth. You don't have to fix anything. I just didn't want to lie to you anymore.

Your friend (who is fine, just not amazing),
Naveen

qa.q: Where does Naveen eat lunch most days at the new school?
qa.a: In the library, most days.

qa.q: Why did Naveen first tell Yash the school was amazing?
qa.a: Naveen was afraid Yash would feel sorry for Naveen or see Naveen as a loser, so the loneliness stayed hidden.

qa.q: What could Yash do after reading this email?
qa.a: Yash could thank Naveen for being honest, give Naveen a call, and keep in regular touch without rushing to fix things.

qa.q: If you were Yash, how might this email feel?
qa.a: It might sting that Naveen hid the truth, but it would also feel like a gift of trust from an old friend. 🤍

grounding: A teen writes to a close friend, taking the risk of dropping a brave front and admitting loneliness.

passage: "So, Simran, you asked about the hardest thing I did this year. It wasn't boards. It was one evening at Sneha's terrace. All my friends were talking about the trip to the hills, and I kept saying I'd 'check dates.' Truth was, my dad had lost his job in March and there was no money for trips. I'd been pretending for months: new excuses, fake busy. That evening I just... said it. My hands were shaking. I said, 'Guys, I can't afford it, and I've been lying because I was ashamed.' Nobody spoke for a second. Then Sneha said, 'Rukmini, why didn't you tell us?' and someone suggested a picnic at the lake instead. I cried a bit on the way home, but lighter, you know?"

qa.q: What had happened to Rukmini's dad in March?
qa.a: He had lost his job.

qa.q: How can you tell that telling the friends felt risky for Rukmini?
qa.a: Rukmini's hands were shaking, and Rukmini admits to months of shame and excuses.

qa.q: What could Rukmini's friends keep doing to support Rukmini?
qa.a: They could keep choosing low-cost plans like the lake picnic and check in quietly, without making money the centre of every talk.

qa.q: How might Sneha have felt when Rukmini spoke up?
qa.a: Sneha seems surprised and a little hurt that a friend carried this alone, but eager to help, asking why Rukmini hadn't told them.

grounding: A teen recounts opening up to friends about a hidden family hardship and how it deepened the friendship.

passage: I'm Damini, and I sit behind Yogesh in the Friday circle our class teacher runs. Usually he makes jokes when it's his turn. This Friday he didn't. He stared at the floor for a long time, and his leg kept bouncing. Then he said his father lost his job two months ago and that he's been pretending everything is normal because he didn't want anyone feeling sorry for him. His voice went thin at the end. Nobody laughed. I didn't know what to do, so I just said, 'Thanks for telling us.' A couple of others nodded. At lunch he sat with us instead of on the back bench. He seemed lighter, or maybe just tired. I'm honestly not sure which.

qa.q: How long ago did Yogesh's father lose his job?
qa.a: Two months ago.

qa.q: What might Yogesh's bouncing leg suggest before he spoke?
qa.a: It suggests he was nervous about the risk of telling the class something so personal.

qa.q: How could the class teacher support Yogesh after this?
qa.a: The teacher could check in with him privately, thank him for trusting the group, and keep the circle a place where no one mocks what is shared.

qa.q: How does Damini see the change in Yogesh at lunch?
qa.a: Damini notices he seems lighter or tired, but admits not being sure what he feels.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking the risk of dropping his joking cover to share something painful with classmates.

passage:
Monday: Chaitanya typed 'can we talk?' to Shalini and deleted it three times. For months he had been pretending the move to the new school was easy. It wasn't. He ate lunch in the library most days.
Wednesday: On the steps after tuition, he finally said it. 'I'm not okay here. I don't really have anyone except you.' His ears burned. Shalini didn't laugh. She was quiet, then said, 'I thought you didn't need anyone. You always seem so sorted.'
Saturday: She texted him a photo of a chess club notice: 'I'll come to the first one with you 🙂'. He saved the photo. For the first time in weeks, he didn't dread Monday.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya eat lunch most days?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya's ears burn when he spoke?
qa.a: He felt exposed and embarrassed, since admitting he wasn't okay was a big emotional risk.

qa.q: What helped Chaitanya's openness pay off, and what could he do next?
qa.a: Shalini listened without laughing; next he could go to chess club with her and keep telling her honestly how things are.

qa.q: How did Shalini's picture of Chaitanya change?
qa.a: She had thought he was sorted and didn't need anyone, and learned he was actually lonely.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager moving from hiding loneliness to risking honesty with a friend, and what followed.
